content: 1. It is essential to ensure that appropriate corrective and preventive actions are implemented to address any identified issues effectively. 2. Regular in-service refresher training is critical for enhancing the knowledge, skills, and attitudes of healthcare providers, while also offering opportunities for ongoing support. 3. Manufacturers of in vitro diagnostics (IVDs), or their economic operators such as suppliers, distributors, or agents, must provide in-service training and troubleshooting support when product issues or adverse events arise. 4. National authorities should consider developing standardized curricula for HIV testing and other aspects of HIV care and treatment, tailored to various testing settings. 5. Certification of HIV testing providers should be considered as an incentive to reinforce the quality of HIV testing activities. 6. In Brazil, the use of technology in training the healthcare workforce has significantly increased the coverage of HIV testing. 7. Expanding access to HIV diagnosis, particularly through rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), is a key strategy of the Brazilian Ministry of Health to achieve the 90–90–90 target by 2020. 8. In 2017, the Ministry of Health distributed over 12 million RDTs, a 23-fold increase compared to 2005, when RDTs were first adopted as a public health policy. 9. To meet the growing demand, the number of healthcare workers trained to conduct HIV testing using RDTs was increased. 10. Considering Brazil's vast geography, with 5,570 cities, and the need for alternatives to on-site training, a free distance-learning course called TELELAB was introduced. 11. TELELAB offers online courses on sexually transmitted infection (STI) diagnosis, including video lessons and instruction manuals. For areas with limited internet access, the course is available on DVD by post. 12. Upon completing the course, professionals receive a certificate after passing an exam with a score of 70% or higher. 13. Sixty-one percent of certified providers are nurses. 14. In 1,943 municipalities observed, 72% of healthcare professionals resided outside the capital, many in remote and rural areas without access to laboratory services. 15. TELELAB has improved access to HIV diagnosis by enabling healthcare professionals, especially nurses, to enhance their HIV testing skills. 16. With more qualified professionals, the Ministry of Health was able to increase the annual distribution of RDTs. 17. Building on its success, TELELAB will be expanded nationwide through a mobile phone application. 18. Regulation of IVDs is a critical component of health systems and directly impacts the quality of HIV testing. 19. The level of scrutiny during pre-market review depends on the product's risk classification, the country's needs, available resources, and the implementation of a national regulatory framework. 20. Pre-market assessment, as per national regulations or legislation, is a necessary step before authorizing the marketing of IVDs, including those for HIV. 21. Pre-market assessment involves controls related to product quality, safety, and performance. 22. Many countries lack the legal framework or resources for effective IVD regulation. 23. To address this gap, WHO conducts prequalification assessments of IVDs likely to be used in resource-limited settings, especially point-of-care diagnostics. 24. WHO independently reviews the quality, safety, and performance of these IVDs and encourages national programs to prioritize WHO-prequalified IVDs during pre-market approval and product selection. 25. WHO prequalification follows a standardized procedure to determine if a product meets its requirements, including dossier review, quality management system inspection, and independent performance evaluation. 26. Post-market surveillance is essential to monitor and detect any quality, safety, or performance issues once a product is on the market. 27. All stakeholders, including end-users, manufacturers, regulators, and testing laboratories, have specific roles in post-market surveillance, but the ultimate responsibility lies with the manufacturer. 28. WHO has issued specific guidance on post-market surveillance of IVDs, emphasizing both reactive and proactive approaches. 29. Reactive surveillance occurs after an adverse event, such as a false-negative test result, is reported. 30. Proactive surveillance identifies potential product problems before they result in adverse effects, such as through lot testing or literature reviews. 31. Manufacturers must record complaints in their system and reassess the risk associated with continued use of the IVD. 32. If the risk is deemed unacceptably high, manufacturers may take corrective actions, such as recalling defective lots. 33. End-users are often the first to detect issues with IVDs and should report problems to manufacturers and economic operators. 34. National authorities may also support complaint reporting and conduct risk-based post-market surveillance. 35. WHO manages a complaint-reporting system for IVDs and oversees investigations and corrective actions by manufacturers. 36. An IVD may be removed from the WHO prequalified list if quality issues are not addressed adequately. 37. Adverse events can cause direct harm, such as death or serious health deterioration, or indirect harm, such as misdiagnosis or delayed treatment. 38. National authorities should collaborate with professional external quality assessment (EQA) providers to build capacity for proficiency testing and address issues identified through quality activities. 39. EQA is a vital tool for post-market surveillance and identifying testing sites prone to errors that could lead to HIV misdiagnosis. 40. Testing sites should participate in EQA schemes at least once per year to evaluate competence, assess individual performance, and ensure the reliability of HIV testing procedures. 41. National procurement policies should prioritize quality-assured diagnostics and coordinate forecasting and quantification across all implementing partners to prevent stockouts. 42. Accreditation of testing sites ensures recognition of their quality and competence, with ISO 15189 being the most widely applicable international standard. 43. National authorities should consider moving towards accreditation of testing sites within their tiered networks. 44. Quality management systems must apply to all HIV testing services, whether facility-based or community-based/mobile. 45. Site supervisors should be trained in quality management principles to oversee quality activities effectively. 46. The WHO guide for Stepwise Laboratory Improvement Process Towards Accreditation (SLIPTA) provides further information on improving laboratory quality. 47. WHO has issued guidance on procuring IVDs and related laboratory items to support HIV testing programs. 48. Testing sites should maintain up-to-date standard operating procedures and standardized records to ensure quality and consistency. 49. Effective occurrence management involves recording and addressing complaints and implementing preventive and corrective actions. 50. Client satisfaction should be measured, and staff safety ensured through proper waste disposal and decontamination procedures.
